svg.title: Five SSM details that must be decided before the deployment: the group range, SSM mapping, IGMPv3 lite and URD, the resulting mroute table, and why SSM crosses domains easily
svg.desc: Five numbered blocks. One: the SSM range can be changed from 232/8 but should not be, because the range must be identical on every router and every host stack. Two: SSM mapping has a static table, a DNS-based source, and an anycast or URL-based source, and it is a migration tool rather than a design. Three: IGMPv3 lite and URD let the application itself ask for a source without a full IGMPv3 stack on the host. Four: the resulting mroute table has only (S,G) entries, no (*,G), no RP, no register, and no shared tree, which is why an RP outage cannot affect it. Five: SSM crosses domains easily because no RP state has to be shared and no MSDP mesh is needed - only the source address has to be reachable. A bottom band states the single hard prerequisite: IGMPv3 or MLDv2 on every access layer, otherwise the join falls back to (*,G) and the RP returns.
svg.text: SSM removes the RP and inherits five obligations
Each of the five is a decision someone must sign; none of them is a default that will be right by accident.
DETAIL 1
The range can move, but should not
232/8 is the interoperability boundary: host
stacks, OS defaults and other vendors all
assume it.
Change it and every router, every host and
every document must change together.
A custom range buys nothing but a scoped
audit problem.
DETAIL 2
SSM mapping has three sources
Static table: group to source, by hand.
DNS: group to source through a name.
URL or controller: the application tells the
network who the source is.
Mapping is a migration tool for IGMPv2
hosts, not an architecture. It hides the
fact that your hosts cannot do SSM.
DETAIL 3
IGMPv3 lite and URD
The application, not the OS stack, sends the
source-specific request. Useful with set-top
boxes and appliances that will never be
upgraded.
Cost: the application owns group membership,
so a crashed app leaks a join.
Decide who owns the join before you deploy.
DETAIL 4
What the mroute table looks like
One entry. No (*,G) beside it.
No RP in the path, no register state, no
shared tree, no switchover event.
An RP outage cannot touch this entry.
That is the operational argument for SSM.
DETAIL 5
Why SSM crosses domains easily
No RP state has to be shared, so no MSDP
mesh and no rendezvous agreement between
domains.
Only two things must be true: the source
address is reachable, and 232/8 is routed.
Cross-domain becomes a routing problem,
not a multicast-protocol problem.
THE ONE HARD PREREQUISITE
IGMPv3 or MLDv2 on every access layer
One IGMPv2 hop turns the join into (*,G), the RP comes back into the path, and the state model you designed for disappears.
Verify it by command, per VLAN, before rollout: the version is visible in the snooping table and in the mroute flags.
